title: Quarrels (Sn 4.11)
hookLine: read it: where do quarrels come from? from what is dear
tomorrow: everyone in the thread is sure they're right. so which one is?

lines: THE FRONT SEAT. THE LAST SLICE.
WHERE DOES A QUARREL COME FROM?
cards: The front seat. The last slice. Whose family gets the holiday this year.

The fights look petty from outside, and they never feel petty from inside. The eleventh poem in the chapter of eights doesn't ask who started it. It asks something better: where does a quarrel come from?
Then it keeps asking, and before that?

teach.b: In paraphrase from the Sutta Nipata, someone asks: where do quarrels and disputes come from, with grief and sorrow, stinginess, pride and slander?
The answer: from what is dear.
And what is dear comes from desire. Desire comes from what's pleasant and unpleasant. And those come from contact, the meeting of the senses with the world.
The poem keeps going, a chain of questions, each one stepping further back. Here's the part worth repeating tonight. Quarrels don't start with the harsh word.
They start with something someone holds dear.
Which means the two people fighting hardest might love the very same thing.
Back in the block on death, grief came from what is dear. Now quarrels do too. The root isn't a bad person.
It's a dear thing, held tight. Find the dear thing, and the other person stops looking like an enemy.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the questions of this poem as a reflection on conflict, tracing a dispute back through what each person holds dear; the chapter of eights is studied for its teaching on letting go of quarrels over views.

o: fights that grow out of what each side holds dear
formal debates held between rival teachers
angry words spoken only by strangers

games.q: two weeks of poems — tap the pairs.
p: gone like a dream on waking

s: quarrels start because someone in them is a bad person
the poem traces them to what is dear, not to a villain.
the poem traces what is dear back to desire, and desire to pleasant and unpleasant
a chain of questions: dear, desire, pleasant and unpleasant, contact.
the poem starts by asking who started the quarrel
it asks where quarrels come from, and keeps asking what came before.

games.q: your parents argue every year about whose grandparents to visit for the holidays. tracing it like the poem, where does it start?
o: from what's dear: each wants their own family honored.
from stubbornness: one of them just likes to win.
from money: the trips cost too much to make twice.
games.why: the poem starts the trail at what is dear. stubbornness and money may be real, but underneath them, each parent loves a family and wants it honored.

practice: Write one recent quarrel at the top of a page, in a few words. Under it, write what was dear to you in it, and then what might have been dear to the other person. Keep asking quietly, and before that?
Let the trail lead where it leads until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Quarrels: in this poem, they grow from what is dear, which is why people who fight hard can be holding the very same thing.

orig.note: Pali: quarrel. The poem is the Kalahavivāda Sutta, on quarrels and disputes.

carryVoice: Keep this close: from what is dear; under the fight, look for the love. Two weeks of poems and endings, done.
